name: Heap
tagline: Instrument explicit first-party events and avoid automatic capture of unrelated user behavior

pricing.notes: Pricing is sales-led; canonical monthly amount is null.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 10,000 sessions/month, 6 months data history, and 1 project/environment

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: Session-based usage estimate after installing the snippet; 12 months data history and 1 project/environment
tiers.notes: No public dollar price; Heap generates an estimate from observed usage.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Custom session volume, 1 year data history, and 3 projects/environments
tiers.notes: Quote only; extra history and additional projects are paid add-ons.

tiers.name: Premier
tiers.limits: Custom session volume, 1 year data history, and unlimited projects/environments
tiers.notes: Quote only; extra history remains an add-on.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 10,000 sessions/month, 6 months data history, and 1 project/environment
pricing.billingTerms: free plan + usage-estimated Growth + custom Pro/Premier contracts; public monthly/annual terms not disclosed
pricing.hiddenCosts: Session Replay, Heatmaps, Error Analysis, Heap Activate, Heap Connect, extra data-history years, and extra Pro projects are add-ons; server-side events consume capacity at 30 events = 1 session after the included contractual allowance.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Heap, instrument explicit first-party events and avoid automatic capture of unrelated user behavior. The hard boundary is automatic capture engine, identity graph, data science, governance, and enterprise operations, plus data pipeline reliability and analytical depth.
coreLoopDIY: Instrument explicit privacy-conscious first-party events, avoid automatic capture of unrelated user behavior, answer a small set of product questions, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: automatic capture engine, identity graph, data science, governance, and enterprise operations
moatNotes: data pipeline reliability and analytical depth
ongoingBurden: event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Heap because teams pay because analytics must keep collecting and remain trustworthy while the product changes underneath it. The recurring cost buys event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Umami
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source privacy-focused web analytics platform.

alternatives.name: Mixpanel Free
alternatives.desc: A transparent event stream with funnels and retention, free up to a million monthly events.

facts.install: Create a hosted project and add a Mixpanel SDK or tracking snippet
facts.dataFormat: Structured events and user profiles are stored in Mixpanel's managed cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: It requires deliberate event instrumentation and cannot recreate Heap's retroactive analysis of automatically captured interactions.
facts.setupBlocker: The software installs cleanly, but meaningful use starts with designing an event taxonomy and instrumenting the product

alternatives.name: OpenPanel
alternatives.desc: Event analytics and user timelines without automatic snooping; ClickHouse administration is the trade.

facts.install: Create a hosted account or run the self-host installer and Docker stack
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment uses PostgreSQL for account data, ClickHouse for event data and Redis for cache and queues; hosted data lives in OpenPanel's service
facts.gapVsPaid: It depends on explicit events and does not provide Heap's automatic capture history for retroactive questions.
facts.setupBlocker: None for the hosted free tier; self-hosting requires Docker, DNS or a reverse proxy and several persistent services

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.desc: Explicit events, funnels and retention without being forced to autocapture the rest of a person's life.

facts.install: Create a PostHog Cloud project or use the hobby self-host script on a Linux server
facts.dataFormat: The self-hosted stack splits analytics, transactions, queues and recordings across ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis and object storage; cloud data lives in PostHog's managed regions
facts.gapVsPaid: It can autocapture, but its retroactive data engine and schema-governance workflow are less polished than Heap's.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting is an unsupported, resource-heavy multi-service stack requiring serious operations work

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.desc: Small, explicit event analytics with funnels and retention, hosted on infrastructure you control.

facts.install: Create an Umami Cloud account or deploy the Node application with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment stores analytics and account data in PostgreSQL; Umami Cloud stores it in Umami's managed service
facts.gapVsPaid: It is lightweight explicit-event analytics with no equivalent to Heap's automatic capture and retroactive history.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting requires Docker or Node hosting and a PostgreSQL database

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Pro plan and a single-product first-party analytics DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Heap in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: instrument explicit privacy-conscious first-party events, avoid automatic capture of unrelated user behavior, answer a small set of product questions, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Ship a lightweight browser SDK for page views and explicit custom events.
Create projects, API keys, environments, event names, and a documented event schema.
Ingest idempotently, filter obvious bots, truncate IP data, and avoid fingerprinting.
Build dashboards for visitors, sessions, funnels, retention, sources, pages, and events.
Expose filters by date, environment, device, country, referrer, and selected properties.
Add retention controls, raw-event export, deletion, health checks, and backup instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out cross-site identity graphs.
Deliberately leave out session replay and automatic DOM capture.
Deliberately leave out warehouse-scale reverse ETL and enterprise governance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
